analysis.one_liner: Orders federal energy regulators to study and report on protecting households from AI data center power costs.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote and the full Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously, 44-0, and now awaits a floor vote before the current Congress ends.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the federal agency that oversees wholesale electricity markets, to hold a technical conference within 90 days of any enactment on ways to shield homes and small businesses from rising electric bills caused by huge electricity users like AI data centers. Utilities, state regulators, and ratepayer advocates would take part. Within 180 days after the conference, the Commission must send a report with recommendations and best practices to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Energy Committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and small businesses on electric bills. Large data centers built for artificial intelligence draw enormous amounts of power, and critics say utilities spread the cost of new generation and transmission across all customers, raising bills for people who never asked for the data centers. The bill creates a formal federal process for designing rate structures that put those costs on the large users instead. Consumer and ratepayer advocates would also gain a seat at an official federal forum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and small businesses on electric bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires FERC to convene a Commissioner-led technical conference on strategies and rate structures for protecting residential and small commercial ratepayers from increased costs tied to large loads, including AI data centers [S2].
Requires a report to House and Senate energy committees with recommendations and best practices from the conference, due within 180 days after the conference concludes [S2].
Guarantees ratepayer advocates, state regulators, and utilities a formal role in the discussion alongside the data centers and transmission providers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the study leads to new rate structures, the cost would fall on large electricity users - data centers and other big industrial customers - who could no longer shift as much of their infrastructure cost onto ordinary bills. In its current form the bill itself costs almost nothing; it funds a conference and a report, not new rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data centers and other large power users

drawbacks.text: The bill requires only a conference and a report - no rule, no rate change, no cap. Holding a technical conference does not lower anyone's electric bill, and FERC could hold the conference and issue recommendations that nothing obligates utilities or states to follow [S2].

If rate structures do eventually shift large-load costs onto data centers, some economists argue those costs can still leak back to consumers through higher prices for cloud services and AI products, and utilities warn blunt cost allocation could complicate grid planning - a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to overburdened households is real but indirect and unguaranteed: the bill starts a process rather than delivering a protection. The direct cost is trivial. Its value depends entirely on whether the conference and report actually lead FERC, utilities, or states to change rate structures; a skeptic would call it a statement bill, while a supporter would call it a necessary first step toward making the biggest power users pay their own way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill passed its House subcommittee by voice vote and the full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported by a unanimous 44-0 vote, but the full House has not voted on it yet and the current Congress runs until early January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, with four original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and its Subcommittee on Energy [S4].
The Subcommittee on Energy considered and marked up the bill on June 24, 2026, and forwarded it to the full committee in amended form by voice vote [S4].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee held markup sessions on July 20 and 21, 2026, and ordered the bill reported by a vote of 44-0, with no member voting against it [S4].
24 members - 23 of the 217 House Democrats and 1 of the 223 House Republicans - are listed as cosponsors [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained materially yet, because the bill has not become law and would only start a process if it did. Data centers and utilities continue operating under existing rate structures, while household bills keep rising; the concrete gain so far is momentum for the bill's supporters and ratepayer advocates, who advanced it through committee without a single dissenting vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; supporters gained momentum

sides.party_line_note: Support so far is bipartisan: the committee reported it 44-0 with no votes against, and the 24 cosponsors include 23 Democrats and 1 Republican [S3, S4].

industries.note: The bill targets the way large data-center loads raise electric bills for everyone else; a conference and report costs them little today, but the process is explicitly aimed at designing rates that shift those costs onto them. Their interest in keeping costs spread across all ratepayers runs against households in this fight.

Utilities must participate in the conference, and any resulting rate structures could limit their ability to recover large-load infrastructure costs from the general rate base. They currently benefit from spreading those costs across all customers, which raises household bills.
The bill gives them a guaranteed seat at a federal technical conference alongside utilities and data centers, a platform they rarely get at that level.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has unanimous committee support and a 44-0 vote, which makes a House floor vote - possibly under a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills - plausible before the Congress ends in January 2027. Even if the House passes it, it would then need Senate action in the final months of the session; a bill that only requires a conference and a report could still make it, but most House bills at this stage die without a Senate vote.
